text: What problem would you keep working on if no one paid you?
evaluation: For interviewers: filters intrinsic motivation from compliance. Specific problem beats abstract domain.

text: What is the last thing you built or shipped that you are proud of, and what part of it was you?
evaluation: The 'what part of it was you' clause separates contribution from association.

text: What is the last thing you built or shipped that you are not proud of, and why?
evaluation: Refusal to name anything is itself a flag. Watch for blame distribution.

text: Tell me about a time you changed your mind because of someone more junior than you.
evaluation: Listen for whether the example exists. Many candidates have none.

text: Tell me about a time you held a position that turned out to be wrong, and how you discovered it.
evaluation: Discovery method is the data: own thinking, evidence, peer, time. 'I haven't been wrong' is disqualifying.

text: What is a piece of feedback you received in the last year that changed how you work?
evaluation: Recency matters. If the last useful piece of feedback was years ago, dig deeper.

text: What kind of feedback do you find hardest to accept, and what helps?
evaluation: Self-awareness about reception is more useful than generic 'I love feedback' answers.

text: Walk me through a decision you made recently with incomplete information.
evaluation: Listen for: the information gap, the framework or instinct used, what they would do differently knowing what they know now.

text: What is a small decision you spent too much time on, and what does that tell you?
evaluation: Self-awareness about decision-energy allocation. Common in over-thinkers and perfectionists.

text: What is a big decision you spent too little time on, and what was the cost?
evaluation: Counterpart. Both errors deserve airtime.

text: What does a great manager do, in concrete behaviour, not in abstractions?
evaluation: Force the specifics. 'Empowers' is not a behaviour. 'Removes one thing from my plate per week' is.

text: What does a bad manager do that you've adapted to without realising?
evaluation: Naming the adaptation is the first step to undoing it.

text: What is one thing about your last team that you would bring to your next?
evaluation: Surfaces what they value about culture. The specifics tell you their actual operating model.

text: What is one thing about your last team that you would never bring to your next?
evaluation: Listen for venting versus considered judgement. Both are useful, distinguishably.

text: What kind of work makes you lose track of time?
evaluation: The shape of flow tells you what role design suits them.

text: What kind of work makes you watch the clock?
evaluation: Pair with wk015. Both shapes are needed in any role; the ratio matters.

text: What is one skill you are deliberately practising right now?
evaluation: Active practice beats passive aspiration. 'I should learn X' isn't an answer.

text: What is one skill you have stopped practising that you used to be good at?
evaluation: Honest answers reveal trade-offs. Listen for whether the loss was conscious.

text: What kind of person do you become when a project is going badly?
evaluation: Self-awareness in failure mode is rare and valuable.

text: What kind of person do you become when a project is going well?
evaluation: Some people degrade in success more than in failure. Worth knowing.

text: Describe a conflict at work where you turned out to be wrong.
evaluation: If they can't, ask why. Real careers contain such moments.

text: Describe a conflict at work where you turned out to be right but handled it badly.
evaluation: The 'right but badly' frame is harder to deflect. Watch for whether they can hold both truths.

text: What is the meeting you have been avoiding scheduling?
evaluation: Avoided meetings often hold the highest-leverage information.

text: What is one thing on your to-do list that has been there for over a month?
evaluation: Investigate why. Often it's misclassified, mis-sized, or someone else's.

text: What is one part of your job that has changed shape without you renegotiating it?
evaluation: Scope creep. Useful before salary or role conversations.

text: What part of your work, if it disappeared tomorrow, would you not miss?
evaluation: Subtraction question. The honest answer is rarely the one in their official duties.

text: What part of your work, if it disappeared tomorrow, would feel like a real loss?
evaluation: Counterpart. The shape of these together is your role.

text: What is your first move when you don't know what to do?
evaluation: Categories: think, search, ask, write, draft, sleep on it. None wrong; the absence of any is.

text: What is your last move before declaring something done?
evaluation: Quality habits live here. Listen for: review, test, write-up, hand-off, sleep on it.

text: What does a good week look like, hour by hour, for you?
evaluation: Force specifics. Ideal-week answers reveal genuine working preferences.

text: What does a bad week look like, hour by hour, for you?
evaluation: Also useful. The negative description often clearer than the positive.

text: What kind of teammate are you in your worst week?
evaluation: Honesty here predicts how a team will weather a downturn together.

text: What kind of teammate are you in your best week?
evaluation: Pair with wk032. Both deserve specifics.

text: What is one assumption you make about new colleagues that you've been wrong about?
evaluation: Bias self-awareness without the rehearsed framing. Look for actual surprise stories.

text: What kind of work do you do best alone, and what do you do best with one other person?
evaluation: The 'one other' clause separates real solo work from real collaboration.

text: What kind of work do you do best in a group, and is there work you avoid doing in groups?
evaluation: Honest avoidance is healthier than performed enthusiasm.

text: What is the last thing you taught someone, and how do you know they learned it?
evaluation: The 'how do you know' clause separates teaching from telling.

text: What is the last thing you learned from someone, and how did they teach it?
evaluation: Method matters as much as substance. Note the credit-giving instinct.

text: What is one piece of work you outgrew before you left it?
evaluation: Outgrowth without departure is one of the most expensive career patterns.

text: What is one piece of work you left before you outgrew it?
evaluation: Counterpart. Both kinds of mistiming exist.

text: What has your career taught you about your own ambition that surprised you?
evaluation: The surprise frame matters. Pre-rehearsed ambition is usually borrowed.

text: What is one ambition you have outgrown without grieving?
evaluation: Quiet pivots deserve their own naming.

text: What is one ambition you have outgrown that you still grieve?
evaluation: Both are normal. Acknowledging grief releases its grip.

text: What is the most expensive mistake you have made at work?
evaluation: Watch for ownership versus theatrical confession. Both miss the point.

text: What is the most expensive mistake you have prevented at work?
evaluation: Often invisible work. People who can name one usually can name several.

text: What is one role you took for the wrong reasons, and what were they?
evaluation: Ego, money, fear, status — knowing your own pulls is half the work.

text: What is one role you turned down that you would not turn down again?
evaluation: Hindsight without bitterness is a sign of integration.

text: What does success in this role look like in 90 days?
evaluation: For interviews. Hiring side: gauges judgement; candidate side: clarifies expectations early.

text: What does failure in this role look like in 90 days?
evaluation: More useful than the success version. Failure is more diagnostic.

text: What would you need from your manager to do your best work here?
evaluation: Specific asks beat 'autonomy and trust'. Force the concrete.

text: What would you not need from your manager that you've been given before, that drained you?
evaluation: Useful both ways. Surfaces past mismatches without naming names.

text: What kind of culture exhausts you, even if it's well-intentioned?
evaluation: Honest fit answers. 'Move fast' culture exhausts some thoughtful candidates; 'consensus' exhausts some operators.

text: What kind of culture brings out your best work?
evaluation: Pair with wk052. The negative is often more honest than the positive.

text: What is one question you wish you had been asked in your last interview?
evaluation: Hands the candidate the keys. Strong candidates have one ready.

text: What is one question you didn't get a satisfying answer to from us, today?
evaluation: For candidates evaluating employers. Re-ask now while it's free.

text: What is one thing about this team that, if you joined, you would push to change in your first six months?
evaluation: Boldness without arrogance. The shape of the answer is more telling than its accuracy.

text: What is one thing about this team that, if you joined, you would protect?
evaluation: Pair with wk056. Reveals what they noticed and valued.

text: What part of your previous job did you wish someone had pushed you out of, sooner?
evaluation: Many of us stayed too long in roles. The unprompted answer is more useful than the polished narrative.

text: What is the most inconvenient truth about how you work?
evaluation: Mornings, focus blocks, slow ramps, late afternoons. Honest constraints beat heroic claims.

text: What is one strength of yours that would surprise your last manager?
evaluation: Tests whether they have visibility into their own under-used capacities.

text: What is one weakness of yours that your last manager would name immediately?
evaluation: If the answer matches the rehearsed-weakness format, dig deeper.

text: Tell me about a project where the politics mattered more than the work.
evaluation: Listen for whether they navigated, ignored, or were eaten by the politics.

text: Tell me about a project where you read the politics wrong.
evaluation: Counterpart to wk062. Vital for senior roles.

text: What does it mean, to you, to be senior in this kind of work?
evaluation: Their seniority thesis. Listen for whether it includes responsibility for others' growth.

text: What kind of work do you no longer want to do, even if you can?
evaluation: Mature answer. The specific 'no longer' is more credible than blanket refusals.

text: What kind of work would you do for free, that you currently get paid for?
evaluation: Watch for honesty. Many roles contain a small core of pure love.

text: What kind of work would you only do for serious money, and how serious?
evaluation: Useful for compensation conversations and for self-knowledge about pull versus push.

text: What is your honest answer to 'why are you leaving' that you wouldn't put in writing?
evaluation: For candidates: privately. The honest answer is the answer.

text: What is the part of your job you would automate first, given the tools?
evaluation: A craft question. The answer reveals what they consider toil versus craft.

text: What is the part of your job you would never automate, even if you could?
evaluation: Counterpart. The protected core is often the actual job.

text: Tell me about a time you went over your manager's head, and was it the right call?
evaluation: Senior calibration. Both 'never had to' and 'often' are flags.

text: Tell me about a time you blocked someone above you, gently, and how it landed.
evaluation: Reveals managing-up skill. Most people have one example if pressed.

text: What is the best thing your last team did that you didn't initiate?
evaluation: Credit-giving instinct check. Subtle but reliable.

text: What is the best thing your last team did that you did initiate, and how did you make sure it stuck?
evaluation: Initiation without follow-through is theatre. The 'stick' clause is the test.

text: What does 'good enough' look like in your craft, and when do you push past it?
evaluation: Operators answer fast; perfectionists struggle here. Both are useful in the right role.

text: What is one habit of yours that ages well in a career, and one that doesn't?
evaluation: Self-modelling about long-arc fit. Rare and valuable.

text: What kind of feedback would your last team be relieved you got from us?
evaluation: An angle that bypasses self-presentation. Even partial honesty here is gold.

text: What kind of feedback would your last team defend you against?
evaluation: Reveals what others have observed but candidate underestimates.

text: What is one piece of your career you'd skip if you could, and what would you keep?
evaluation: Edit-the-narrative question. The 'keep' part is often surprising.

text: What is your relationship to deadlines, when no one is checking?
evaluation: Honest answer matters more than the impressive one.

text: What is your relationship to deadlines that someone else owns?
evaluation: Reliability for others is often higher than for self. Useful to name.

text: What is the longest you've held a private opinion at work that you later turned out to be right about?
evaluation: Listen for: did they speak it eventually? Why or why not?

text: What is the longest you've held a private opinion at work that you later turned out to be wrong about?
evaluation: Counterpart. Asking both prevents the heroic narrative.

text: Walk me through a budget you owned. How accurate did it turn out to be?
evaluation: Concrete numerical accountability. Beats abstract claims of business sense.

text: Walk me through a hire you regret, and what you learned about your own evaluation process.
evaluation: Senior question. The lesson about *self* matters more than the lesson about the hire.

text: Walk me through a hire you are proudest of, and what you couldn't have predicted.
evaluation: Humility marker. The 'couldn't have predicted' clause filters retrospective genius.

text: What does your day look like when you are working on something genuinely hard?
evaluation: Concrete texture. Reveals real working style, not aspirational one.

text: What does your day look like when you are working on something boring you must finish?
evaluation: Tedious work is most of work. Their relationship to it matters.

text: What is one thing you have changed your mind about, in your craft, in the last three years?
evaluation: Craft humility. If nothing has changed, why?

text: What is one thing in your craft you keep doing that may already be obsolete?
evaluation: Tools and methods age fast. The willingness to ask is more important than the answer.

text: What is the best meeting you have ever been in, and what made it that?
evaluation: Tells you their model of good collaboration. Watch for verbs.

text: What is the worst meeting you have ever been in, and what would you have done differently?
evaluation: Practical leadership signal. The 'what you would have done' is the test.

text: What is one piece of slack in your current role that no one is using?
evaluation: Capacity awareness. Different from being overworked.

text: What is one piece of slack in your current role that you have started using without permission?
evaluation: Permissionless initiative. Look for whether the use produced value or risk.

text: Tell me about a time you said no to your boss, and how you set it up.
evaluation: The set-up matters more than the no. Reveals communication craft.

text: Tell me about a time you said yes to your boss when you should have said no.
evaluation: Pair with wk095. Both deserve airtime.

text: What is the one number, in your work, you watch most carefully?
evaluation: If they have one, that's a strong signal of operator-mindedness. If they have ten, that's a different signal.

text: What is the one number you have stopped watching that you maybe should not have?
evaluation: Lapsed attention. Often where small problems became big ones.

text: What kind of recognition do you actually need to keep going, beyond money?
evaluation: Specific. 'Public' versus 'private', 'from peers' versus 'from manager', 'verbal' versus 'a real chance at the next thing'.

text: What is the next move in your career, in your own words, with no audience?
evaluation: Closing. Strip away the resume version. The honest sentence is usually short.
